title: Handover
description: The body of the signed POST /v1/dispatches/<dispatch_id>/handover, application/json: the starter asks for the run key and the input of the job it started for the dispatch. Before calling handover, the starter has satisfied itself that the job asking is the one it started for this dispatch. It passes the run key to that job alone, and keeps it no longer than that. How it proves the job is the starter's business. For a dispatched run, the handover is the run's registration, https://qory.dev/contracts/forager/v1/run-registration.schema.json: the control plane registers the run, as a registration through a gateway by the node pool, when it answers the handover, and the answer's run_key is that registered run's run key, bound to the claimed run and to the gateway the node pool's choice resolved to, as the run key's run_id and gateway name them. The job never registers a dispatched run itself. The control plane refuses, under any key, a registration at the run endpoint whose run_id is that of a run of this contract, waiting for a node pool, claimed, handed over or ended, with the signed 409 run_id_used, decided first: before the stored answer to a repeated registration and before the instance limit. The Forager contract gives the run endpoint's other causes and their order. So a dispatched run's run key comes only from the handover. What a registration would carry, the run's id, its labels, what it is about and its attach window, the control plane sets from the dispatch, the run's id being the claimed run's run_id. The registered run's instance id, the run key's instance_id, is the run's id, the claimed run_id, so each dispatched run is a new instance, which holds the slot of the pool's instance limit it took at the claim, claim.schema.json. A run key is handed over at most once per run: the answer, handover-answer.schema.json, is given once, sent with Cache-Control: no-store and never cached, and a second handover is refused, 409 handed_over. Once its handover is answered, a dispatch never goes back to the queue: a release after it ends the run, release.schema.json. A dispatch_id that is unknown, or that is of a node pool the key does not serve, is refused 403 forbidden, with the same signed body as an unknown pool, so nobody learns whether an id exists; the control plane decides this before any 409 or 410. The signature with the pool's access key and that check authorise the request, not the id. A handover before dispatched is refused, 409 not_dispatched; after the lease lapsed and the dispatch went back to the queue with the same run, 409 lease_expired, and the starter then stops the job it started for that dispatch; after the dispatch ended because its work item was closed or undone, 410 gone. After the 403 and these state checks, a handover at which the node pool's choice resolves to no gateway, or to direct, is refused, 409 no_gateway, as a claim is. After it, the dispatch stays claimed until its lease lapses, so the starter may send the handover again, built anew, while the lease lasts; after that, the lease-lapse rule above applies. A refused handover registers no run and takes no new slot of the pool's instance limit: the dispatch keeps the slot it took at the claim until that slot is freed. It is signed with the pool's access key as definitions.schema.json describes. The control plane refuses a time more than 300 seconds from its clock, either way, or a request whose signature it has already seen, with an unsigned 401. A member this schema does not define is refused, invalid_request.

version.description: The document format. The control plane refuses a version it does not read.

time.description: When the starter built the body, RFC 3339 in UTC with whole seconds. The control plane refuses a time more than 300 seconds from its clock, either way, with an unsigned 401.
